Agentic AI systems are increasingly deployed in hospitals clinical decision support systems (CDSS), where multiple specialized agents negotiate over patient-care recommendations. This distributed negotiation introduced as “many hands” problem: overrides, disagreements and consensus-building can become opaque, and responsibility for erroneous outcomes cannot be clearly attributed. Existing healthcare AI ethics guidance largely address single system, output facing behavior and does not formally govern internal multi-agent negotiation. This study first synthesizes nine established game theoretic and mechanism design paradigms-including Prisoner's Dilemma, Bayesian games, signaling games, principal-agent theory, Stag Hunt, repeated games, VCG style mechanism design, Shapley value, and Chicken/Hawk-Dove mapping: their applicability and limitations for ethically accountable multi-agent CDSS negotiation. Building on this synthesis, we purpose the Musical Chairs Coalition Convergence Game (MC3G), a novel coalition-based framework that governs agent negotiation with a bounded protocol clock, a reputation-weighted convergence rule, and a mandatory escalation-to-human safety valve for any agent that fails to converge. As a proof-of-concept illustration of the framework’s qualitative behaviour rather than a clinically validated evaluation, we ran a synthetic simulation, non-inferential toy simulation (four agents, 2,000 cases per condition, varying strategic agent prevalence) comparing MC3G against naïve majority voting and reputation-only baseline.
